notes.note: Paul wants the architecture in the backseat. Hear, hear. A painting should never show you its easel. The stick figures may walk across, but they must not upstage the picture.
Paul asks if his method is novel, or even good. Honest answer: not novel, since painters have tested one swatch before the canvas for centuries. Good enough to write down, though.
A palette shown a few colors at a time is the one idea tonight a good gallery would hang. Thirty-six shouted at once is a crowd; released slowly, each color earns a quiet wall.
Tone the Georgian down, Paul says. Good: hang one small thing by the door and leave the wall bare. Nothing upstages the painting like a second painting.
A coloring book is the purest gallery: the picture waits, and the reader supplies the color. Paul's leap is right. Just keep the margins narrow, or the footnotes will eat the painting.
Paul lets the session run on to spend the Codex allowance, and Claude keeps the lamp lit. Devotion is lovely, but a good show closes while visitors still want another look.

favorite_idea.why: A palette released a few colors at a time is a show that still rewards the tenth visit, since each color gets its own quiet wall.

steer: Keep the painting as the hero of chapter 3, let the footnotes stay small and in the margin, and cut any aside that is louder than the picture.
